title: Regional drying over the Western U.S. driven by enhanced atmospheric subsidence amid global moistening from 1980 to 2020
abstract: As the global climate has warmed anthropogenically over the past decades, the atmosphere across most of the globe has experienced significant moistening, except for a "moistening hole" (MH) -like change over the Western U.S. This regional anomaly since 1980 is at odds with the forced response of climate models to global warming in this region. Here, through analysis of a wide array of observations and water-tagging enabled simulations, we find that atmospheric forcing originating from the North Pacific contributes to the MH. A barotropic high-pressure circulation trend over the North Pacific, driven by observed sea surface temperature cooling in the tropical Eastern Pacific, enhances atmospheric sinking over the Western U.S. through equatorward cold air advection. This intensified atmospheric descent suppresses precipitation and weakens land-sourced evaporation, which are critical for replenishing atmospheric moisture in the region. We suggest that focusing on low-frequency changes of atmospheric vertical motion may offer insights into assessing and projecting climate stress and drought risks posed by long-term atmospheric moisture deficits in arid regions.
problem: Existing climate models fail to reproduce the observed atmospheric drying over the Western U.S., a regional anomaly known as the "moistening hole," which contrasts with the widespread moistening expected from global warming and seen in model simulations.
method: This study integrates analyses of reanalysis datasets, large-ensemble simulations, AMIP runs, and water-tagging experiments to identify the circulation trends and moisture sources responsible for the long-term drying trend over the Western U.S. amid global moistening.
task: The task is to identify the physical mechanisms driving the anomalous atmospheric drying trend over the Western U.S. from 1980 to 2020, which contrasts with the widespread moistening observed elsewhere due to global warming.
innovation: This study reveals that the anomalous drying trend over the Western U.S. from 1980-2020 was driven by enhanced atmospheric subsidence and reduced moisture recycling, which was triggered by sea surface temperature cooling in the tropical Eastern Pacific.

To more directly validate the role of boundary SST forcing in shaping the recent MH over the U.S. West, we examine the atmospheric response to a prescribed SST cooling anomaly using control and sensitivity runs from two AGCMs (Fig. 7). All model configurations (for example, global SST and sea ice, anthropogenic forcing) are identical between the control and sensitivity run, except that the latter includes an additional SST-cooling pattern imposed in the tropical Eastern Pacific (Methods). The difference between the two runs over the 30-year integrations highlights, in a qualitative sense, the important role of tropical Pacific cooling in driving an anomalous barotropic high over the North Pacific, which favors an MH-like pattern over the Western U.S., although associated atmospheric drying is stronger in CAM5 than in ECHAM5.

To better understand the observed hydrological cycle in North America from 1980 to 2020 and to examine atmosphere-ocean-land interactions, we use iCESM1.2 (at 1.9° × 2.5° resolution) in this study45, which allows us to quantify the impacts of observed atmospheric and boundary forcing on moisture, precipitation, and key land processes across North America.
Following a standard procedure (Eq. 3) of the NCAR Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) system, we apply full nudging (a = 1) to constrain the model to evolve as closely as possible to ERA5.

In addition, iCESM1.2 includes a water tagging function, which enables the tracking of atmospheric moisture from its source regions to its ultimate sinks. This capability allows us to monitor the complete lifecycle of water vapor, from evaporation to precipitation, along with intermediate hydrological processes, offering insights into both local and remote sources of moisture and precipitation variability

Under Setting 1, we first conduct a 41-year (1980–2020) iCESM simulation with global nudging and 54 predefined tagging regions spanning the globe. Each tagging region covers 60° longitude × 20° latitude, with regions sequentially labeled west-to-east within a latitude band before progressing from south to north.

To refine our understanding of moisture sources over North America, we conduct a second simulation focusing on regions 35 and 41, which cover Central and North America (10°–50°N, 240°E–300°E). These regions are subdivided into 24 smaller domains (10° × 10° resolution) to enable finer-scale differentiation of moisture sources.
